report:
Conclusion: the claim is broadly supported, with an important qualifier: tenofovir is an add-on to timely newborn hepatitis B vaccine ± HBIG, not a replacement. In mothers with chronic HBV and high viral load, residual transmission can occur despite immunoprophylaxis; lowering maternal HBV DNA late in pregnancy reduces that risk.

The pivotal randomized trial enrolled HBeAg-positive mothers with HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL, started tenofovir disoproxil fumarate at 30–32 weeks, and reported lower transmission than placebo (about 5% vs 18% intention-to-treat; 0% vs 7% per-protocol) when infants received standard immunoprophylaxis (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa1508660). A WHO-commissioned Lancet Infectious Diseases systematic review found peripartum antiviral prophylaxis reduced MTCT in high-risk pregnancies without a clear safety signal (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(20)30586-7/abstract). WHO therefore recommends tenofovir from 28 weeks for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with high viral load (≥200,000 IU/mL) where testing is available, alongside infant vaccination (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/978-92-4-000270-8). AASLD/IDSA similarly recommends tenofovir at gestational week 28 for HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL regardless of HBeAg status (https://www.guidelinecentral.com/guideline/10618/).

Caveat: absolute benefit depends on baseline risk and quality/timing of birth-dose vaccine and HBIG; where immunoprophylaxis is optimal, added benefit may be small.
